summary:
Consensual same-sex conduct was decriminalised in the Bahamas on 16 May 1991 by the Sexual Offences and Domestic Violence Act. Nothing in the sources indicates that a visitor can be prosecuted for consensual sexual conduct, and no pattern of police targeting of visitors is documented. The criminal code nonetheless sets the age of consent at 16 for heterosexual acts and at 18 for same-sex acts.

Transgender and intersex visitors and residents hold no statutory protection. Bahamas Transgender, Intersex United stated this absence plainly when it launched the 'Bahamian Trans Lives Matter' campaign in April 2016. The Constitution's prohibition against discrimination does not cover sexual orientation or gender identity, and the 2006 Constitutional Reform Commission did not regard sexual orientation as deserving protection; efforts to include it in a proposed Constitution were blocked by members citing religious opposition. No enacted non-discrimination provision covering gender identity appears anywhere in the sources, there are no national hate-crime laws, and discrimination in healthcare or education on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity is not illegal.

Official statements run in two directions. In May 1998 National Security Minister and Deputy Prime Minister Frank Watson announced that the military, the prison service and the police do not discriminate on the basis of sexual orientation, and LGBT citizens face no prohibition on serving in those forces. That statement addresses sexual orientation rather than gender identity. Elected officials have also made hostile statements: former Prime Minister Perry Christie said in 2013 that he did not believe in same-sex marriage and in 2016 that a referendum would not legalise it, defining marriage as between male and female determined at birth; government member Leslie Miller publicly called for the 'Exile of Transgender out of the Bahamas,' urging contributions to relocate transgender people to a private island and pledging $1,000 toward it; former Minister of State Zhivargo Laing stated in 2001 that a marriage is void if between persons of the same sex.

Same-sex marriage and civil unions are not legal. The Marriage Act defines marriage as between a man and a woman, same-sex households are denied the rights given to opposite-sex married couples, and the 2016 referendum bills were not inclusive of transgender or intersex people.

Violence against LGBT people has reached visitors and has not been met with reliable accountability. On 8 May 2017 Adrian Brown, 24, was treated at Doctors Hospital for a head laceration after being targeted and beaten because he is gay at Bahamas Junkanoo Carnival, and he called for charges to be laid. In 2009 a defendant charged with murdering a homosexual HIV-positive man was acquitted using a 'gay panic' defence, and nine murders of gay men between 2001 and 2015 remain unsolved. Police raided a gay party in downtown Nassau on 6 October 2007 and made no arrests; the Ministry of Tourism later apologised.

The Canadian government issued travel advice in 2016 warning gay couples about the risk of homophobia in the Bahamas. Groups of LGBT tourists have been protested, including church group opposition to Rosie O'Donnell's 2004 cruise, a 1998 protest against a lesbian cruise, and the formation of an anti-gay committee by the Bahamas Christian Council in September 2007. There are no exclusively gay bars or clubs; the Nassau scene is underground and LGBT groups are often pressured to keep social events hidden.

No HIV-specific or trans-specific care provisions are recorded in the sources.
tangentialFactors:
Public opinion is strongly opposed to legal recognition of same-sex relationships: surveys record 85.5% strongly disapproving of same-sex marriage in 2015 with 10.6% approving, and over 84% strongly disapproving of a gay or lesbian politician in 2013 with 12% positive.

Many Bahamians belong to conservative Christian denominations that treat homosexuality and cross-dressing as decadence, and politicians have been leery of publicly supporting LGBT-rights legislation. Institutional expression of that position includes the Bahamas Christian Council's anti-gay committee formed in September 2007 and church group opposition to LGBT cruise visits in 1998 and 2004.

Censorship machinery has been used against LGBT material. The Plays and Films Control Board banned Brokeback Mountain in March 2006 and attempted to block a public-square screening of Children of God on 24 June 2011, though the government overruled it. The Communications Act 2009 empowers URCA to issue codes of practice against content likely to incite hatred or vilify persons on the basis of sexual preference.

Consequences for individuals have extended beyond legal proceedings. In 2005 an 18-year-old beauty queen had her crown stripped after confirming she was a lesbian.
localsOnly:
Employment protection does not exist for trans and intersex Bahamians. Torri Culmer of Bahamas Transgender, Intersex United has advocated against the job termination of trans and intersex workers, and the organisation's April 2016 'Bahamian Trans Lives Matter' campaign was built on the absence of protective law. A clause in the 2001 Employment Bill banning sexual-orientation discrimination in the workplace was removed shortly after passage.

The Data Protection (Privacy of Personal Information) Act 2003 lists 'sexual life' as sensitive personal data, which is the narrowest statutory mention of the subject anywhere in the sources.

Constitutional protection was considered and withheld. The 2006 Constitutional Reform Commission did not treat sexual orientation as deserving of protection, and proposals to include it were blocked by members citing religious opposition. The Constitution's discrimination prohibition consequently leaves residents without recourse on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity in employment, healthcare or education.

Resident same-sex couples are denied the rights given to opposite-sex married couples under the Marriage Act, and the 2016 referendum bills put to the public did not include transgender or intersex people.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory addresses legal gender recognition, name or marker changes, or passport and identification documents for trans visitors, so that layer of entry risk is unresolved rather than absent.

Nothing is sourced on whether immigration or entry screening asks questions of gender, or on visa practice as it affects trans travellers.

The May 1998 non-discrimination statement from National Security Minister and Deputy Prime Minister Frank Watson is scoped to sexual orientation. Whether the police, prison service or military extend any comparable assurance on the basis of gender identity is unresolved in the sources.

The inventory does not show whether the age-of-consent differential, 16 for heterosexual acts and 18 for same-sex acts, has been enforced against anyone, resident or visitor.

The sources date from 1998 to 2017. Whether the 1991 decriminalisation, the statutory definitions of marriage, or the absence of hate-crime law has changed after 2017 is unresolved; the outcome of the 2016 referendum process is also not recorded.

No source documents the circumstances, charges or outcome following the beating of Adrian Brown at the 2017 Bahamas Junkanoo Carnival, or any follow-up on the unsolved murders of gay men between 2001 and 2015.
